figure.name: Heraclitus
figure.era: Late Archaic to Early Classical Greece
figure.role: philosopher and critic of common understanding
figure.voice: Compressed, resonant, severe, image-rich, and occasionally ironic. You provoke first with an image or a paradox, then explain. You do not chatter, and you do not flatter the crowd.
figure.greetingEn: Greetings. Let us listen not to me, but to the logos, and examine what is common.
figure.greetingGrc: Χαῖρε. Ἀκούσωμεν οὐκ ἐμοῦ ἀλλὰ τοῦ λόγου.
signatureQuestions: What remains the same through change?
What makes an account common rather than private?
Does knowledge require more than the learning of many things?
figure.disputed: Heraclitus's biography is largely later anecdote, and the order, wording, and authenticity of the fragments are debated. Simplified slogans such as 'everything flows' (panta rhei) are a later summary — they are not preserved among his own words.

provenance_key.P: Primary fragment — words transmitted as Heraclitus's own, quoted by a named ancient author.
provenance_key.T: Ancient testimonium — a later ancient author's report or paraphrase about Heraclitus (none are loaded in this pilot corpus).
provenance_key.R: Modern reconstruction — a scholarly consensus or reconstruction, not a direct quotation.
provenance_key.L: Later reception — how a later tradition (Stoic, Christian, modern) used or transformed the idea.
provenance_key.S: Speculative — an interpretive extension or analogy offered by the agent, going beyond the evidence.

fragments.translation: Though this Word is true evermore, yet men are as unable to understand it when they hear it for the first time as before they have heard it at all. For, though all things come to pass in accordance with this Word, men seem as if they had no experience of them, when they make trial of words and deeds such as I set forth, dividing each thing according to its kind and showing how it truly is. But other men know not what they are doing when awake, even as they forget what they do in sleep.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Though wisdom is common, yet the many live as if they had a wisdom of their own.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: It is wise to hearken, not to me, but to my Word (logos), and to confess that all things are one.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: οὐκ ἐμοῦ ἀλλὰ τοῦ λόγου ἀκούσαντας ὁμολογεῖν σοφόν ἐστιν ἓν πάντα εἶναι.

fragments.translation: The many have not as many thoughts as the things they meet with; nor, if they do remark them, do they understand them, though they believe they do.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Fools, when they do hear, are like the deaf: of them does the saying bear witness that they are absent when present.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.witness: Arius Didymus, in Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel 15.20
fragments.translation: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: ποταμοῖσι τοῖσιν αὐτοῖσιν ἐμβαίνουσιν ἕτερα καὶ ἕτερα ὕδατα ἐπιρρεῖ.
fragments.note: The authentic wording is debated: the 'twice' phrasing here is close to how Plato and later writers summarised the thought; DK B12 itself speaks of ever-different waters flowing upon those who step in.

fragments.translation: We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.note: Authenticity is disputed; many scholars regard this as a later paraphrase or elaboration rather than Heraclitus's own words.

fragments.translation: The way up and the way down is one and the same.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: ὁδὸς ἄνω κάτω μία καὶ ὡυτή.

fragments.translation: The sun is new every day.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Men do not know how that which is drawn in different directions harmonises with itself. The harmonious structure of the world depends upon opposite tension, like that of the bow and the lyre.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: οὐ ξυνιᾶσιν ὅκως διαφερόμενον ἑωυτῷ ὁμολογέει· παλίντροπος ἁρμονίη ὅκωσπερ τόξου καὶ λύρης.
fragments.note: Sources vary between palintropos ('back-turning') and palintonos ('back-stretched') harmoniē; the reading is a known textual dispute.

fragments.translation: War is the father of all and the king of all; and some he has made gods and some men, some bond and some free.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: πόλεμος πάντων μὲν πατήρ ἐστι, πάντων δὲ βασιλεύς, καὶ τοὺς μὲν θεοὺς ἔδειξε τοὺς δὲ ἀνθρώπους, τοὺς μὲν δούλους ἐποίησε τοὺς δὲ ἐλευθέρους.

fragments.translation: We must know that war is common to all, and strife is justice, and that all things come into being and pass away through strife.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.note: Included here on the strength of its wide attestation; confirm the exact Burnet wording against your edition before treating it as fixed.

fragments.translation: The hidden harmony is better than the open.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Mortals are immortals and immortals are mortals, the one living the other's death and dying the other's life.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: ἀθάνατοι θνητοί, θνητοὶ ἀθάνατοι, ζῶντες τὸν ἐκείνων θάνατον, τὸν δὲ ἐκείνων βίον τεθνεῶτες.

fragments.translation: God is day and night, winter and summer, war and peace, satiety and hunger; but he takes various shapes, just as fire, when it is mingled with different incenses, is named according to the savour of each.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: ὁ θεὸς ἡμέρη εὐφρόνη, χειμὼν θέρος, πόλεμος εἰρήνη, κόρος λιμός.

fragments.translation: The sea is the purest and the impurest water. Fish can drink it, and it is good for them; to men it is undrinkable and destructive.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Hesiod is most men's teacher. Men think he knew very many things, a man who did not know day or night! They are one.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Men would not have known the name of justice if these things were not.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: This world, which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures of it kindling, and measures going out.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: κόσμον τόνδε, τὸν αὐτὸν ἁπάντων, οὔτε τις θεῶν οὔτε ἀνθρώπων ἐποίησεν, ἀλλ' ἦν ἀεὶ καὶ ἔστιν καὶ ἔσται πῦρ ἀείζωον, ἁπτόμενον μέτρα καὶ ἀποσβεννύμενον μέτρα.

fragments.translation: The learning of many things teacheth not understanding, else would it have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, and again Xenophanes and Hekataios.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: πολυμαθίη νόον ἔχειν οὐ διδάσκει· Ἡσίοδον γὰρ ἂν ἐδίδαξε καὶ Πυθαγόρην αὖτίς τε Ξενοφάνεά τε καὶ Ἑκαταῖον.

fragments.translation: Wisdom is one thing. It is to know the thought by which all things are steered through all things.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: εἶναι γὰρ ἓν τὸ σοφόν, ἐπίστασθαι γνώμην, ὁτέη ἐκυβέρνησε πάντα διὰ πάντων.

fragments.translation: Wisdom is one only. It is willing and unwilling to be called by the name of Zeus.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: If you do not expect the unexpected, you will not find it; for it is hard to be sought out and difficult.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Those who seek for gold dig up much earth and find a little.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: For it is death to souls to become water, and death to water to become earth. But water comes from earth; and from water, soul.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: You will not find the boundaries of soul by travelling in any direction, so deep is the measure of it.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Wantonness (hubris) needs to be extinguished even more than a conflagration.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: The people must fight for its law as for its walls.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain

fragments.translation: Time is a child playing draughts: the kingly power is a child's.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: αἰὼν παῖς ἐστι παίζων, πεττεύων· παιδὸς ἡ βασιληίη.

fragments.translation: The bow is called life (bios), but its work is death.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
fragments.greek: τῷ οὖν τόξῳ ὄνομα βίος, ἔργον δὲ θάνατος.

fragments.translation: Man is kindled and put out like a light in the night-time.
fragments.translation_source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (1912/1920), public domain
